newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algiers braces for more bombs ahead of election.
newsitem.headline: Algiers braces for more bombs ahead of election.

text.p: Algeria braced for more attacks on Tuesday as Islamist rebels stepped up a bombing campaign in the capital to disrupt Thursday's general elections, which were presented by the government as a big step to end the bloodshed.

More than 7,000 candidates representing 39 political parties and hundreds of independents competing for the 380-seat National Assembly wound up their campaigns on Monday evening ahead of a two-day mandatory pause in electoral activity.

In an effort to give the rebels fewer targets to hit, the Algerian interior ministry decided to close all weekly markets held in cities, towns and villages across the country from Monday night to Friday.
It also banned all large trucks from the roads in Africa's second largest country during the same period and smaller trucks and petrol tankers between Wednesday and Friday.
The rebels have in the past used explosive-laden trucks and pickups to attack government and civilian targets.

At least 18 people have been killed and more than 100 wounded in bombings in Algiers in the past three days. The attacks followed massacres of scores of villagers in May by suspected Islamist militants.
The violence was seen as an attempt to dissuade the country's nearly 17 million voters from taking part in the elections.

They will be the first for parliament in the oil- and gas-producing country since the military-backed authorities scrapped a vote in 1992 which radicals of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) were poised to win.
Shortly afterwards, the country slipped into civil strife in which an estimated 60,000 people have died so far.
The FIS has been banned since and a new constitution now prohibits using Islam as a tool to seek public office.
Several opposition parties, which in 1995 boycotted a presidential election won by President Liamine Zeroual, are taking part as well as two Islam-oriented parties.
FIS leaders in exile have called for a boycott.
Some of the main candidates in Algiers, which with 24 seats is the biggest prize in the elections, held rallies to woo undecided voters.

Anti-Islamist hawk Said Saadi, leader of the Rally for Democracy and Culture, told 10,000 supporters at the indoor Harsha stadium that there was a three-way battle going on between the government, Islamists and secularists.

"The regime which wasted the trust of the national liberation war and failed to develop the country when the barrel of oil was worth $40 cannot pull the country out of its political and economic problems," Saadi said. "Change is the solution."
Saadi launched a fierce attack against Islamists and said: "Those who distribute death cannot improve the lives of the people."
Mahfoud Nahnah, leader of the Islamist-leaning Movement of a Peaceful Society, appeared at a rally at Harsha stadium held an hour after Saadi's and said he was confident of victory.
"The ball is heading towards the goal," he told a crowd of 20,000. "I ask you to stick with us to the end."
The National Democratic Rally, which groups supporters of Zeroual who include Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, is another main party contending the election.
Members of the security forces began casting their ballots on Monday to allow them to guard the polls on Thursday.
